title: context: cancellation, deadlines, values used sparingly
summary: A context.Context carries a cancellation signal, an optional deadline and a few request-scoped values down the call chain. Every function that does I/O takes it as its first parameter and stops when ctx.Done() is closed.

annotations.note: This select is the whole contract: do the work, but stop waiting once ctx.Done() is closed. net/http, database/sql and pgx do the same inside every call that takes a ctx.
Wrap ctx.Err() with %w, so callers can still ask errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) and tell a timeout from a real failure.
WithTimeoutCause (Go 1.21) attaches a reason. ctx.Err() still reports DeadlineExceeded, so existing checks keep working; context.Cause returns the reason for logs and error messages.

Call cancel on every path, even after success: it stops the timer and detaches the child from its parent. Deferring it on the next line is the idiom, and go vet's lostcancel check reports a dropped CancelFunc.

Cancellation is a request, not a kill. query stops only because it selects on ctx.Done(); a function that ignores its ctx runs to the end regardless. Calling a CancelFunc twice, or from several goroutines, is safe.
When the work beats the deadline, the context never fires and the result comes back as usual.

examples.title: Cancellation flows down the tree; WithoutCancel and AfterFunc

annotations.note: Every With... call wraps a parent, so contexts form a tree. In a server the root is r.Context(), which net/http cancels when the client disconnects or the handler returns.
Canceling cacheCall leaves request and dbCall alone. Cancellation flows from parent to children, never up or sideways.
WithoutCancel (Go 1.21) keeps the parent's values but drops its cancellation and deadline. Use it for work that must finish after the request is gone, and give that work a timeout of its own.

AfterFunc (Go 1.21) runs the callback in a new goroutine once the context is canceled. It is how you connect a blocking call that takes no ctx, for example closing a connection to unblock a read. The closed channel only fixes the output order.
One call reached every descendant: the hour-long dbCall is canceled too. The audit context isn't, and still carries the user value.

examples.title: Values with unexported key types and typed accessors

annotations.note: The key's type is unexported, so only this package can construct the key. Another package's key with the same underlying 0 has a different type and can't collide with it.
Export typed helpers, not the key, as the context docs recommend. Callers never see the any, and a missing value yields the zero value rather than a failed type assertion.

Values are for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries: a request ID, a trace span, the authenticated user. What a function needs to do its job belongs in its parameters, where the compiler checks it.
A key matches only if both type and value are equal, so authKey("user"), logKey("user") and the plain string "user" are three different keys. That is why the docs warn against built-in key types.

use_cases: Per-request deadlines in HTTP handlers: derive from r.Context() so a disconnected client stops the database query it started
Outgoing calls with a budget: context.WithTimeout around an HTTP request, a pgx query or a gRPC call
Graceful shutdown: signal.NotifyContext cancels a root context on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, and everything derived from it winds down
Request-scoped metadata that middleware adds and logging reads: request ID, trace span, authenticated user
strengths: One convention across the standard library and the ecosystem: net/http, database/sql, pgx and gRPC all take ctx first, unlike Java, where each API has its own timeout and interrupt story
Cancellation propagates through the whole call tree from one cancel() call, including into goroutines started deeper down
Deadlines compose: a child can only shorten its parent's deadline, so a 100ms handler budget can't be exceeded by a callee asking for 5s
weaknesses: Cooperative only: code that never checks ctx.Done() or passes ctx on can't be cancelled, and nothing in the type system tells you
ctx is threaded by hand through every signature, which is noisier than the implicit propagation of Python's contextvars or Java's ThreadLocal
Values are untyped (any) and invisible in signatures, so they turn into hidden parameters when overused

pitfalls.title: Storing a Context in a struct
pitfalls.detail: The context docs say to pass it explicitly to each function instead. A stored ctx outlives the request it belonged to, and callers can't give individual calls their own deadline.
pitfalls.bad: type Repo struct { ctx context.Context; db *pgxpool.Pool }
pitfalls.good: func (r *Repo) FindUser(ctx context.Context, id int64) (User, error)

pitfalls.title: Using context.Background() deep in the call chain
pitfalls.detail: It cuts the chain: the request's deadline and cancellation no longer reach the query. Background belongs in main, tests and top-level setup; elsewhere pass the ctx you were given, or context.TODO() while refactoring.

pitfalls.title: Optional parameters in context values
pitfalls.detail: A page size or a feature flag hidden in the context is a parameter the compiler can't check. Use a function argument or an options struct.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting cancel
pitfalls.detail: Without cancel, a WithTimeout child and its timer stay alive until the timeout fires or the parent is canceled; with WithCancel, until the parent is canceled. go vet's lostcancel check reports it.
pitfalls.good:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, time.Second)
defer cancel()

quiz.q: A child context is canceled. What happens to its parent?
options: Nothing: cancellation only flows to descendants
quiz.why: Canceling a context cancels it and its children; parents and siblings are untouched.

quiz.q: ctx was created with WithTimeoutCause(parent, d, myErr) and the deadline passed. What does ctx.Err() return?
quiz.why: Err keeps reporting DeadlineExceeded so existing checks still work; context.Cause(ctx) returns myErr.

quiz.q: A function receives ctx but never selects on ctx.Done() and never passes ctx on. What does canceling ctx do to it?
quiz.why: A context only signals. Work stops when code observes Done or hands ctx to an API that does.

body:
## Concept

A `context.Context` is an immutable value that carries three things down a call chain:
a **cancellation signal** (`Done()` returns a channel that is closed on cancel), an
optional **deadline**, and a few **request-scoped values**. You never modify a context;
you derive a child from it:

- `context.WithCancel(parent)` returns a child and a `cancel` function.
- `context.WithTimeout(parent, d)` / `WithDeadline(parent, t)` cancel automatically.
- `WithCancelCause` (Go 1.20) and `WithTimeoutCause` / `WithDeadlineCause` (Go 1.21)
  record why; `context.Cause(ctx)` reads it back.
- `context.WithValue(parent, key, val)` attaches one value.

When a context is canceled, every context derived from it is canceled too. After that,
`ctx.Err()` returns `context.Canceled` or `context.DeadlineExceeded`.

The convention is strict: anything that does I/O or may block takes
`ctx context.Context` as its **first parameter** and passes it on.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS**: `AbortController`/`AbortSignal` is the closest match. `signal` ≈ `ctx`,
  `controller.abort(reason)` ≈ `cancel(cause)`, `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` ≈
  `WithTimeout`, and `fetch(url, { signal })` ≈ passing `ctx` to `http.NewRequestWithContext`.
- **Java**: there is no single equivalent. `Thread.interrupt()` is per thread,
  `Future.cancel(true)` per task, and every API has its own timeout parameters.
  `context` is one mechanism used everywhere, and it's explicit rather than a flag
  on the thread.
- **Python**: `asyncio` cancels a task by raising `CancelledError` inside it. Go has no
  exceptions to inject: the callee has to check `ctx.Done()` or `ctx.Err()`.
  `contextvars` covers the values part.
- **C/C++**: closest to passing a cancellation token around by hand, as in C++20's
  `std::stop_token`, with deadlines built in.

## How it works

`Done()` returns a channel that is **closed**, never sent on, when the context is
canceled. A closed channel is ready for every receiver, so one `cancel()` wakes any
number of goroutines selecting on `<-ctx.Done()`. That's why the cancellation check is
a `select` case, the pattern from the previous lesson.

Deadlines only get shorter. `WithTimeout(parent, 5*time.Second)` under a parent that
expires in 100ms still expires in 100ms. A handler's budget therefore holds no matter
what its callees ask for.

For incoming HTTP requests, `r.Context()` is canceled when the client's connection
closes, when an HTTP/2 request is canceled, or when `ServeHTTP` returns. Deriving every
query's context from it means a disconnected client stops the database work it started.

## Design notes

Context is plumbing, so keep it boring:

- First parameter, named `ctx`, never stored in a struct, never `nil` (use
  `context.TODO()` if you're unsure which context to use).
- `context.Background()` belongs at the top: in `main`, in tests (or `t.Context()`,
  Go 1.24) and in long-lived background loops.
- Call `cancel` on every path, usually with `defer` on the next line.
- Values only for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries, behind an unexported
  key type with typed accessors. If a function needs a value to do its job, it's a
  parameter.
- Pick the timeout where the budget is known, usually at the edge (the handler or the
  job runner), and let deeper layers inherit it rather than invent their own.

`errgroup` (lesson 6) builds on this: its context is canceled as soon as one goroutine in
the group fails, so its siblings stop early.
